newsitem.title: USA: Gehrig uniform buyer a relative newcomer to collecting.
newsitem.headline: Gehrig uniform buyer a relative newcomer to collecting.

text.p: The man whose group bought Lou Gehrig's uniform last month for a record $306,000 is a relative newcomer to collecting who got interested when he happened into a store selling old autographs.
"I didn't even know things like this existed until about six years ago. Then I got involved with a vengeance," David Bowen said by telephone from his office in Columbus, Ohio.

Bowen, 40, is married with two sons and has run his own advertising and promotion business since 1982. But it was not until he bought an autograph of former Dodger pitching great Don Drysdale that he got hooked.
"Baseball is still the national pastime, I don't care where the popularity is, and nothing gets more American than Lou Gehrig on that day," he said.

That day was July 4, 1939, when an ailing Gehrig mesmerised the nation with his "Luckiest Man Alive" speech at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx. The uniform Gehrig wore that day is the one Bowen and four partners bought on June 28.

"The man was bigger than life when he played and he's still bigger than life now that he's passed away," Bowen said, calling the 1939 speech "probably the single greatest speech ever delivered in sports."
Baseball experts agreed, saying that while the price was the highest ever for a uniform, it was attached to a remarkable piece of history.

The highest price for any piece of baseball memorabilia was the $640,500 that a mint-condition Honus Wagner card fetched at auction last year. The card, from around 1909, is the best of the 50 or so known to exist, baseball collectors and historians said after the sale. But there was only one Gehrig uniform from the day the Iron Horse gave his speech.
"This is probably the greatest piece of memorabilia in all of sports," Bowen said, referring to the uniform.

The day of the auction, Bowen and his partners made an opening bid of $181,500, which held until late in the afternoon. After other bids started coming in, they raised their bid to $200,000, and again to $220,000.
"At 7:05, while I was at my sister's wedding reception, I got a call that we'd gotten bumped again. I called back later and we bumped it back," he said.
The other bidder at that point in the mail, fax and telephone auction was a surgeon who had been called away on an emergency, Bowen said.

As the story was told to him, Bowen said, the surgeon's wife called him at the hospital and he came out of surgery and told her he had more important things to do and could not focus on the auction just then.

"Don't you just love the guy's priorities?" Bowen said, adding he got a call at 12:45 on Sunday morning telling him his group had won the bidding for the uniform, which was auctioned by Robert Edward Auctions, the nation's leading baseball collectibles house.
"I was up until 3 in the morning calling people. I was elated. We had a party the next day," Bowen said.
Bowen's group plans to display the uniform on five Sundays starting on Sept. 14 at Cool Stuff, a sports and entertainment memorabilia store he owns with a partner in Columbus.

"It's gonna be a lot of fun," said Bowen, who was born in Lakeland, near Cleveland. "It's an investment piece. I've told everyone I think it's a million dollar piece. I absolutely believe it's more valuable than the Wagner card.
"I can't think of any single uniform I'd take over it."
With the uniform in hand, the Cincinnati Reds fan can return his attention to his other hunt.

"I'm on what I call the quest, which is to get the entire baseball Hall of Fame," he said, referring to autographs. He has all but two of the 232 players, managers and others who will be in the hall after this year's induction on Aug. 3.
"Only two guys in the country have the whole collection," Bowen said. "The quest continues."
